title_en: Ending a Tenancy When You Change Jobs
summary_en: What changing employers or losing your work pass means for the clock on your room tenancy.
body_en:
Your work pass is tied to your employer. When that job ends, your pass usually gets cancelled too — and that starts a clock that your room tenancy now has to fit around, whether you planned for it or not.

What happens to your pass

When your employment ends, your employer typically cancels your work pass. You don't automatically have to leave Singapore that same day, but you do need a valid pass to stay legally, so apply for a Short-Term Visit Pass (STVP) through MOM's eService if you're still in Singapore and your pass has been cancelled.

How much time you typically get

  • Employment Pass holders can usually get an STVP valid for up to 90 days after cancellation.
  • Work Permit holders are generally issued a Special Pass valid for up to 14 days.
  • A general STVP requested through the eService can be granted for up to 30 days, depending on your situation.

What this means for your room

  • Check your tenancy agreement's notice period as soon as you know your job is ending — don't wait for the pass to actually be cancelled.
  • If your pass window is shorter than your notice period, talk to your landlord early. Most would rather know now than be surprised later.
  • If you're starting a new job quickly, your new employer may apply for a new pass — ask if you can stay in the same room while that's processed.
  • Keep copies of your cancellation letter and any STVP approval, in case your landlord or a future employer asks to see them.

Don't let this slip

Overstaying even briefly without a valid pass carries real penalties. Sort out your pass status first, then work out your room's notice period around it — not the other way round.

General guidance, November 2026 — not legal advice. Check current STVP rules on mom.gov.sg.

facts_checked.claim: After a work pass is cancelled, a person still in Singapore should apply for a Short-Term Visit Pass to maintain a valid stay, or risk an overstaying fine
